content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, bounded
10	  `loop`, and dynamic `map` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- a map node inside a loop body expands independently in every iteration
30	  from that iteration's source output, its instances and events belonging
31	  to the iteration they expanded in;
32	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
33	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
34	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
35	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
36	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
37	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
38	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
39	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
40	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
41	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
42	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
43	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
44	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
45	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
46	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
47	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
48	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
49	  set (delivery is at least once);
50	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
51	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
52	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
53	  resumed, periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
54	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy, and a read-only preview
55	  query projects the upcoming trigger times and their inputs.
56	
57	## Requirements
58	
59	- Python 3.11 or newer
60	- no third-party runtime dependencies
61	
62	## Run the service
63	
64	```bash
65	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
66	```
67	
68	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
69	has bound the port.
70	
71	## HTTP API
72	
73	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
74	
75	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
76	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
77	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
78	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
79	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
80	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
81	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
82	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
83	
84	### Tenants and quotas
85	
86	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
87	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
88	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
89	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
90	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
91	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
92	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
93	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
94	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
95	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
96	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
97	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
98	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
99	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
100	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
101	
102	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
103	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
104	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, instance deletion and
105	modification and re-expansion, queue pulls, acknowledgements, and all
106	history and status queries (the schedule change history included), as well as the quota declaration and delete, the quota
107	read and remaining query, the quota change history, the price
108	declaration and price delete, the price read and the price change history, and the usage, bill, and
109	metrics queries. An empty
110	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
111	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
112	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
113	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
114	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
115	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
116	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
117	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
118	the usual `409 conflict`.
119	
120	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
121	hold:
122	
123	```http
124	PUT /quotas
125	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
126	X-Tenant-Id: acme
127	
128	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
129	```
130	
131	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
132	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer, and may additionally
133	carry the optional `growth` object described below; a non-positive,
134	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
135	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Every quota
136	route requires a tenant: declaring, deleting, and reading without
137	`X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty one) is a `400 validation_error`, and an
138	unknown query parameter on the delete or the remaining query is rejected the
139	same way, with the message naming the offending parameter. The response is
140	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
141	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
142	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
143	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
144	
145	Besides the two limits a declaration may carry one optional `growth` object
146	naming an automatic expansion policy for each limited resource. A policy
147	names only the resources it covers, and a resource it omits is never raised
148	automatically. Each named resource must declare exactly a positive integer
149	`step` and a positive integer `cap`, and the cap must not be below the
150	resource's declared limit:
151	
152	```http
153	PUT /quotas
154	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-2
155	X-Tenant-Id: acme
156	
157	{"workflows":10,"executions":100,"growth":{"workflows":{"step":5,"cap":50},"executions":{"step":50,"cap":500}}}
158	```
159	
160	A missing field, an unknown field (inside the policy or beside it), a
161	non-object policy, a resource other than `workflows` or `executions`, or a
162	step or cap that is non-positive, non-integer, boolean, or non-finite is a
163	`400 validation_error`; a cap below the resource's declared limit is rejected
164	the same way. Every such rejection writes nothing. A declaration without
165	`growth` is byte-for-byte the two-limit request above; repeating a declaration
166	replaces limits and policy as a whole, so a declaration that names no `growth`
167	also drops the tenant's previous policy. The declaration response and the
168	quota read include the policy only when one is declared, with each entry
169	listing `step` before `cap` and resources in workflows-first order:
170	
171	```json
172	{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100,"growth":{"workflows":{"step":5,"cap":50},"executions":{"step":50,"cap":500}}}}
173	```
174	
175	```http
176	GET /quotas
177	X-Tenant-Id: acme
178	```
179	
180	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
181	when the tenant has declared none.
182	
183	A tenant can also remove the quota it declared, on the same path with the
184	`DELETE` method and the same calling shape as the other quota writes:
185	
186	```http
187	DELETE /quotas
188	Idempotency-Key: quota-delete-1
189	X-Tenant-Id: acme
190	
191	{}
192	```
193	
194	The body must be exactly an empty object; a non-empty or non-object body, an
195	unknown field, or a non-finite value is a `400 validation_error` that touches
196	no quota. The delete removes the declaration as a whole and leaves no partial
197	write, so a later read gives the same definite empty result as for a tenant
198	that never declared one: the delete response and every following read both
199	return `{"quota":null}`, and the remaining query lists neither resource —
200	neither limit, holding, nor remaining — and repeats with exactly the same
201	result. Deleting the quota of a tenant that never declared one returns that
202	same definite empty result rather than an error. The delete clears only the
203	declaration: it deletes no existing workflow or execution, and data already
204	held stays fully usable. It writes no metering record, so recorded usage
205	counts and bill conclusions already reached stay exactly as they were; later
206	writes simply run without a quota check until the tenant declares again.
207	
208	The delete follows the same idempotency rules as every other write: the
209	`Idempotency-Key` header is required, repeating the same delete with the same
210	key returns the first result and performs no second removal, and reusing a
211	key for another operation — including a quota declaration — in the same
212	tenant is a `409 conflict` that leaves the tenant's quota unchanged. Quotas
213	are scoped per tenant like everything else: deleting one tenant's quota never
214	affects another tenant's declaration or remaining room. A missing or empty
215	tenant and a missing idempotency key are `400 validation_error`, and every
216	failed validation writes nothing — no quota row, no metering record, and no
217	quota or price-table change history.
218	
219	A separate read-only entry point reports how much room the declared quota
220	leaves, with the same calling shape as the quota read:
221	
222	```http
223	GET /quotas/status
224	X-Tenant-Id: acme
225	```
226	
227	Each limited resource gives three numbers — the declared `limit`, the
228	`held` count the quota decision itself uses, and the `remaining` room, which
229	is simply limit minus holding — in that key order, with workflows first and
230	executions second; the same query repeats with the same ordering:
231	
232	```json
233	{"status":{"workflows":{"limit":10,"held":3,"remaining":7},"executions":{"limit":100,"held":12,"remaining":88}}}
234	```
235	
236	Lowering a limit below the current holding reports the `remaining` room
237	truthfully as a negative number; it is neither clamped to zero nor rejected.
238	A tenant that has never declared a quota gets the definite empty result
239	`{"status":null}`, listing neither resource. The query is strictly read-only:
240	it writes no metering record and changes no declared quota, usage, bill,
241	scheduling, approval, or replay conclusion, and another tenant's quota and
242	holdings are never visible and never influence the result. It requires a
243	tenant and accepts no query parameters: a missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id`
244	header, an unknown parameter (named in the error message), or a repeated
245	parameter is a `400 validation_error`, and these rejections write nothing.
246	
247	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the write is admitted
248	once the resource declares a growth policy that can make room: the declared
249	limit is raised in whole steps — the smallest number of `step` increments
250	that admits the write — never past the `cap` and never by a partial final
251	step, and the raised limit commits with the write in the same transaction,
252	so the request succeeds instead of returning a conflict. The expansion
253	changes only the declared limit: it writes no metering record, changes no
254	recorded usage count, and changes no bill conclusion already reached.
255	Repeating the same write with the same idempotency key returns the first
256	result without a second expansion, and reusing that key for another
257	operation is the usual `409 conflict`. Without a policy on the resource, or
258	when no whole-step raise within the cap can admit the write — including when
259	the cap already leaves no room for one more holding — the whole request is
260	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
261	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
262	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
263	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write and leaves the limit
264	untouched: nothing is inserted and previously stored data is unaffected,
265	exactly as for validation failures. The quota read and the remaining query
266	report the raised limit; the remaining query's `remaining` room is computed
267	from it.
268	
269	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
270	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
271	is at its execution limit, a growth policy raises the limit exactly as for a
272	manual creation and the period fires normally; when there is no policy or
273	the cap leaves no room a whole step can reach, the due period creates no
274	execution and the schedule is left unchanged — its cursor,
275	`last_triggered_at`, and `last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the
276	period is settled on a later pass once capacity exists, under the usual
277	per-period idempotence. Delivery history follows the tenant of the execution
278	it belongs to.

280	### Quota change history
281	
282	Every successful quota declaration or delete leaves one change record, so a
283	caller can see exactly when each quota declaration and each removal took
284	effect. A separate read-only entry point returns the tenant's change history
285	with the same calling shape as the price-table change history:
286	
287	```http
288	GET /quotas/history?limit=50
289	X-Tenant-Id: acme
290	```
291	
292	Returns `{"history":[...]}` with the records in ascending order of occurrence
293	time; records sharing one instant are ordered by a stable ascending sequence.
294	Each record is:
295	
296	```json
297	{"sequence":7,"action":"declare","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z","snapshot":{"workflows":10,"executions":100,"growth":{"workflows":{"step":5,"cap":50},"executions":{"step":50,"cap":500}}}}
298	```
299	
300	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant,
301	  shared across both kinds of quota change. It identifies the record across
302	  every query and is never renumbered by a filter or a page;
303	- `action` is `declare` for a quota declaration or `delete` for a removal;
304	- `occurred_at` is the moment the change took effect, an ISO-8601 UTC string
305	  ending in `Z`;
306	- `snapshot` is the complete quota in effect after the change. A
307	  declaration's snapshot is the limits and growth policy that took effect:
308	  the two limits first, `workflows` before `executions`, followed by the
309	  optional `growth` object containing only the resources this declaration
310	  named, each entry listing `step` before `cap`; a declaration without a
311	  growth policy lists no `growth` at all. A delete's snapshot is `null`.
312	
313	The history record is written atomically with the change it describes, in the
314	same transaction as the quota write, so a reader always sees the declaration
315	and its history agree and a declaration or delete rejected by validation, a
316	quota conflict, or an idempotency-key conflict leaves no record. Repeating an
317	idempotent declaration or delete with the same key returns the first result
318	and appends no second record; reusing a key for another operation is the
319	usual `409 conflict` and, again, writes no history. Deleting the quota of a
320	tenant that never declared one still succeeds and still leaves its own
321	`delete` record (with a `null` snapshot), exactly as it returns the definite
322	empty result for the quota itself.
323	
324	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
325	`{"history":[]}`, never an error. The response is one line of compact JSON
326	with the record keys in the order above, full number precision preserved, and
327	a single trailing newline, like every other JSON endpoint.
328	
329	The endpoint accepts an optional action filter, the same optional closed time
330	window the per-record usage query accepts, plus cursor pagination, in exactly
331	the same shape as the price-table change history:
332	
333	```http
334	GET /quotas/history?action=declare,delete&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
335	```
336	
337	- `action` names one action or a comma-separated set of them (`declare` and
338	  `delete`); only records whose action is in the set are returned. A single
339	  value needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown
340	  action is a `400 validation_error`; when `action` is absent every change is
341	  returned;
342	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
343	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
344	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
345	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing
346	  and the definite empty list is returned;
347	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
348	  contains more than that many records;
349	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
350	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
351	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
352	- the action filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
353	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
354	
355	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `action` entry, a
356	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
357	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
358	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
359	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records, and another tenant's history
360	is never visible under any filter. The query is read-only: it appends no
361	history, writes no metering record, and changes no quota declaration, usage,
362	bill, scheduling, approval, or replay conclusion. A quota declaration or
363	delete not participating in this change — reads, the remaining query,
364	scheduling, metering, and billing included — is byte-for-byte unchanged, and
365	no metering record is added. After a replay or a recovery each record's
366	sequence, occurrence time, and snapshot stay exactly as they were first
367	written.

369	### Tenant price tables
370	
371	The bill's baseline unit prices are built in. A tenant may instead declare
372	its own price table on a separate entry point with the same calling shape as
373	the quota declaration:
374	
375	```http
376	PUT /prices
377	Idempotency-Key: price-request-1
378	X-Tenant-Id: acme
379	
380	{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}
381	```
382	
383	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must be a non-empty
384	JSON object giving a map of metered action type to a positive-integer unit
385	price in cents. A non-positive, non-integer, boolean, or non-finite price,
386	an unknown metered type, a missing field (an empty object), an extra field
387	that is not a metered type, or a non-object body is a `400
388	validation_error` that writes nothing. Every price route requires a tenant:
389	declaring, deleting, and reading without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
390	one) is a `400 validation_error`, and an unknown query parameter on the
391	read or the delete is rejected the same way, with the message naming the
392	offending parameter. The response is
393	`{"prices":{"execution_started":200,"workflow_created":1500}}`, with the
394	declared types in ascending type-identifier order.
395	
396	A successful declaration replaces the tenant's price table as a whole with
397	exactly the types given this time; metered types the declaration does not
398	name fall back to the built-in default prices when a bill is taken. The
399	declaration rewrites no recorded usage counts and changes no bill taken
400	before it was made.
401	
402	```http
403	GET /prices
404	X-Tenant-Id: acme
405	```
406	
407	Returns the price table currently declared by the tenant, in ascending
408	type-identifier order, or the definite empty result `{"prices":null}` for a
409	tenant that has never declared one. The stored table lists only the types
410	the declaration named; types left at the default are not copied into it.
411	
412	A tenant can also remove the table it declared, on the same path with the
413	`DELETE` method and the same calling shape as the other price writes:
414	
415	```http
416	DELETE /prices
417	Idempotency-Key: price-delete-1
418	X-Tenant-Id: acme
419	
420	{}
421	```
422	
423	The body must be exactly an empty object; a non-empty or non-object body,
424	an unknown field, or a non-finite value is a `400 validation_error` that
425	touches no price table. The delete removes the table as a whole and leaves
426	no partial write: it is atomic with the declaration and the read, so a
427	concurrent reader sees either the complete old table or no table at all.
428	After it succeeds the tenant no longer holds a declared table, and both the
429	delete response and the following read give the definite empty result
430	`{"prices":null}`. Deleting the table of a tenant that never declared one
431	returns that same definite empty result rather than an error. The delete
432	rewrites no recorded usage counts and changes no bill taken before it was
433	made; afterward both the bill and the bucketed bill price every type at the
434	built-in default, each line still giving the metered type, the actual
435	`unit_price` used, the `count`, and the integer-cent `subtotal`.
436	
437	The declaration and the delete follow the same idempotency rules as every
438	other write: the `Idempotency-Key` header is required, repeating the same
439	declaration or the same delete with the same key returns the first result
440	and performs no second replacement or removal, and reusing a key for
441	another operation — including another price declaration or a price delete
442	— in the same tenant is a `409 conflict` that leaves the tenant's price
443	table unchanged. Price tables are scoped per tenant like everything else: a
444	tenant can never read or delete another's declaration, and another tenant's
445	declaration or deletion never affects this tenant's bill amounts.
446	
447	The bill and the bucketed bill price with the price table in effect **at
448	query time**: a named type uses the tenant's declared price and every other
449	type uses the built-in default. Each returned line still gives the metered
450	type, the actual `unit_price` used, the `count`, and the integer-cent
451	`subtotal`, and the total is exactly the sum of the listed subtotals; types
452	with no matching record are still omitted rather than listed at zero. A
453	declaration affects only later queries — it neither rewrites recorded usage
454	nor revises historical bills — changes no metering, and leaves the bill and
455	usage queries read-only. A delete affects only later queries in the same
456	way: the table is removed as a whole, later bills fall back to the
457	built-in defaults, and recorded usage and already-taken bills stay exactly
458	as they were.

542	### Usage metering and billing
543	
544	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
545	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
546	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
547	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
548	metered action types are:
549	
550	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
551	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
552	  definition;
553	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
554	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
555	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
556	  `schedule_triggered`;
557	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
558	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
559	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
560	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
561	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
562	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
563	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
564	  meters nothing.
565	
566	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
567	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
568	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
569	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
570	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
571	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
572	
573	```http
574	GET /usage
575	X-Tenant-Id: acme
576	```
577	
578	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
579	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
580	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
581	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
582	
583	```http
584	GET /bill
585	X-Tenant-Id: acme
586	```
587	
588	Returns the per-type bill:
589	
590	```json
591	{"bill":{"items":[
592	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
593	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
594	],"total":2100}}
595	```
596	
597	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
598	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
599	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
600	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`. The price used per type is
601	the tenant's declared price when its price table names that type and the
602	built-in default otherwise, read from the table in effect at query time (see
603	[Tenant price tables](#tenant-price-tables)); tenants with no declaration are
604	billed byte for byte as before.
605	
606	Both endpoints accept the same optional query parameters the events and
607	metrics queries accept: an optional metered-type filter and an ISO-8601 UTC
608	timestamp window, each timestamp ending in `Z`, plus an optional fixed time
609	bucket:
610	
611	```http
612	GET /usage?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
613	GET /bill?type=execution_started&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
614	X-Tenant-Id: acme
615	```
616	
617	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them; only
618	  records whose type is in the set are counted. A single identifier needs no
619	  comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered type is a
620	  `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is counted, exactly
621	  as before;
622	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on each usage record's
623	  occurrence time: a record whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted.
624	  When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting
625	  both returns exactly the cumulative result above;
626	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
627	  parameter is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing;
628	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
629	  simply contains no records. Usage then reports the definite empty result
630	  `{"usage":[]}`, and the bill reports an empty `items` list with a `total` of
631	  `0`.
632	
633	The type filter and the time window apply together as an intersection: a
634	record is counted only when its type is named **and** its occurrence time is
635	in the window. A type the filter names but that has no matching record is
636	omitted rather than reported at zero, so a filter that matches nothing gives
637	the same definite empty results as an empty window: `{"usage":[]}` for usage
638	and an empty `items` list with a `total` of `0` for the bill.
639	
640	Both endpoints also accept an optional `bucket` parameter for a fixed-bucket
641	trend summary, so callers never have to pull records and group them
642	themselves:
643	
644	```http
645	GET /usage?bucket=hour&since=2026-09-26T00:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-27T00:00:00.000Z
646	GET /bill?bucket=day&type=execution_started
647	X-Tenant-Id: acme
648	```
649	
650	- `bucket` is exactly `hour` or `day`: `hour` buckets start on the UTC hour
651	  and `day` buckets at UTC midnight, both aligned solely to UTC. An empty or
652	  any other value is a `400 validation_error`, exactly like a repeated
653	  parameter or an unknown query parameter;
654	- when `bucket` is present, usage returns
655	  `{"usage_buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T08:00:00Z","usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}, ...]}`:
656	  the buckets with at least one matching record, in ascending bucket-start
657	  order. Each entry gives its `bucket_start` first — an ISO-8601 UTC string
658	  ending in `Z` at the hour or midnight — followed by `usage`, the per-type
659	  counts inside that bucket in ascending type-identifier order; a type with no
660	  record in the bucket is omitted;
661	- when `bucket` is present, the bill returns
662	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T00:00:00Z","items":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100}, ...],"subtotal":100}, ...],"total":100}}`.
663	  Buckets appear in ascending bucket-start order; each bucket's `items` stay
664	  sorted by ascending type identifier, each line giving the filtered count,
665	  the usual positive-integer `unit_price`, and an integer-cent `subtotal` of
666	  the two, and a type with no matching record is omitted rather than reported
667	  at zero. Each bucket also carries its own `subtotal`, and the window
668	  `total` is exactly the sum of the listed per-bucket subtotals, all amounts
669	  integer cents;
670	- a bucket that holds no matching record never appears, so an empty tenant, a
671	  window with `since` later than `until`, or a filter that matches nothing
672	  returns the definite empty bucket lists `{"usage_buckets":[]}` and
673	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[],"total":0}` — never an error, with the empty bill's
674	  total at `0`;
675	- bucketing applies together with the type filter and the time window as an
676	  intersection: a bucket holds only records whose occurrence time is in the
677	  closed window **and** whose type the filter names. The window keeps its
678	  closed endpoints, its open bounds when either side is omitted, and the
679	  existing rule for when a record's instant falls in it; buckets are simply
680	  the same matching records rolled up to their UTC bucket;
681	- the bucketed queries are read-only like the others: they append no usage
682	  records, change no metering basis or prices, and never alter recorded usage
683	  or billing conclusions — under event replay or recovery the same window,
684	  type filter, and bucket always give the same answer;
685	- omitting `bucket` leaves both queries exactly as before: the same compact
686	  JSON responses with `usage` / `items` shapes, full float precision and the
687	  `-0.0` convention, byte for byte. The parameter introduces no second
688	  protocol and changes no entry point's existing behavior.
689	
690	Only records whose occurrence time falls in the window are counted. Within
691	the window the bill keeps the same basis as always: each present type reports
692	its filtered, windowed count, its usual `unit_price`, and a `subtotal` of the
693	two; items stay sorted by ascending type identifier, and a type with no
694	matching record is omitted rather than reported at zero. The bill's `total`
695	is exactly the sum of the subtotals of the listed items. The query is
696	read-only: it writes no usage records, changes no prices or metering
697	conclusions, and never alters already recorded usage — under event replay or
698	recovery the same window and type filter always give the same answer.
699	
700	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
701	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error` that reveals no usage. Usage and
702	bill data follow the usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see
703	another's records under any type filter or window, and another tenant's
704	records never affect this tenant's counts or totals.

766	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
767	appends no usage records, writes no events, and changes no metering, prices,
768	quotas, or billing conclusions. Records follow the usual tenant isolation, so
769	another tenant's records are never visible under any type filter, window, or
770	page and never affect this tenant's result; replay and recovery leave every
771	recorded sequence, time, and billing conclusion unchanged.
772	
773	### Operational metrics
774	
775	```http
776	GET /metrics
777	X-Tenant-Id: acme
778	```
779	
780	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
781	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
782	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
783	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
784	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
785	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
786	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
787	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
788	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
789	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
790	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
791	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
792	
793	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
794	timestamp ending in `Z`:
795	
796	```http
797	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
798	X-Tenant-Id: acme
799	```
800	
801	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
802	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
803	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
804	  counts every recorded fact;
805	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
806	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
807	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
808	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
809	  result.
810	
811	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
812	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
813	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
814	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
815	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
816	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
817	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
818	completion or termination event.
819	
820	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
821	
822	```http
823	GET /metrics/export
824	X-Tenant-Id: acme
825	```
826	
827	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
828	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
829	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
830	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
831	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
832	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
833	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
834	
835	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
836	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
837	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
838	ordered by ascending label value:
839	
840	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
841	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
842	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
843	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
844	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
845	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
846	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
847	  unlabeled scalar samples.
848	
849	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
850	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
851	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
852	ends with a single newline.
853	
854	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
855	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
856	failures, and schedule triggers:
857	
858	```json
859	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
860	```
861	
862	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
863	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
864	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
865	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
866	  ended for that reason.
867	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
868	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
869	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
870	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
871	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
872	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
873	  another attempt, per node identifier.
874	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
875	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
876	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
877	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
878	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
879	
880	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
881	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
882	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
883	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
884	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
885	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.
886	
887	### Health
888	
889	```http
890	GET /health
891	```
892	
893	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.

895	### Create a workflow
896	
897	```http
898	POST /workflows
899	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
900	
901	{
902	  "id": "order-flow",
903	  "nodes": [
904	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
905	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
906	  ]
907	}
908	```
909	
910	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
911	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
912	
913	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
914	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
915	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
916	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
917	
918	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
919	
920	```json
921	{
922	  "id": "order-flow",
923	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
924	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
925	}
926	```
927	
928	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
929	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
930	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
931	
932	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
933	
934	```json
935	{
936	  "id": "nightly-orders",
937	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
938	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
939	}
940	```
941	
942	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
943	
944	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
945	
946	```json
947	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
948	```
949	
950	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
951	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
952	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
953	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
954	`false`.
955	
956	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
957	
958	```json
959	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
960	```
961	
962	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
963	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
964	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
965	dependencies of its successors.
966	
967	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
968	
969	```json
970	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
971	```
972	
973	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
974	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
975	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
976	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
977	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
978	`retries_exhausted`.
979	
980	A task may instead declare an approval point:
981	
982	```json
983	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
984	```
985	
986	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
987	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
988	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
989	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
990	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
991	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
992	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
993	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
994	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
995	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
996	move the task.
997	
998	### Submit an approval decision
999	
1000	```http
1001	POST /executions/run-1/decision
1002	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
1003	
1004	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
1005	```
1006	
1007	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
1008	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
1009	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
1010	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
1011	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
1012	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
1013	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
1014	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
1015	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
1016	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
1017	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
1018	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
1019	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
1020	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
1021	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
1022	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
1023	404.
1024	
1025	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
1026	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
1027	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
1028	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
1029	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
1030	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
1031	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
1032	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
1033	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
1034	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
1035	shape and event stream.
1036	
1037	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
1038	segment:
1039	
1040	```json
1041	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
1042	```
1043	
1044	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
1045	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
1046	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
1047	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
1048	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
1049	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
1050	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
1051	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
1052	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
1053	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
1054	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
1055	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
1056	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
1057	loop node instead).
1058	
1059	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
1060	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
1061	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
1062	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
1063	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
1064	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
1065	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
1066	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
1067	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
1068	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
1069	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
1070	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
1071	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
1072	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
1073	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
1074	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
1075	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
1076	belong only to their iterations.
1077	
1078	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
1079	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
1080	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
1081	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
1082	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
1083	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
1084	exactly.
1085	
1086	### Dynamic map nodes
1087	
1088	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
1089	recorded array:
1090	
1091	```json
1092	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
1093	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
1094	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
1095	```
1096	
1097	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
1098	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
1099	
1100	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
1101	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
1102	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
1103	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
1104	  the same path syntax as a condition.
1105	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
1106	  expand.
1107	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
1108	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
1109	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
1110	  uses. The template id only names the dynamically expanded instances; it
1111	  may coincide with a declared node id or with another map's template id.
1112	  A map node may also sit inside a loop body, expanding independently in
1113	  every iteration (see "Maps inside loop bodies" below).
1114	
1115	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
1116	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
1117	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
1118	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
1119	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
1120	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
1121	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
1122	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
1123	overwrite another instance.
1124	
1125	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
1126	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
1127	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
1128	become available in the usual way.
1129	
1130	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
1131	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
1132	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
1133	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
1134	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
1135	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
1136	
1137	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
1138	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per retained
1139	instance giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or
1140	`failed`), its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a
1141	permanently failed instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and
1142	the node's single `failure_reason`. A `ready` instance that has been
1143	rewritten by a successful modify additionally carries that rewritten
1144	`input`; every other instance record keeps exactly these fields. The `maps`
1145	field is present only when the bound workflow declares a map node outside
1146	any loop body; every other execution keeps its previous state shape.
1147	
1148	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
1149	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
1150	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
1151	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
1152	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
1153	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
1154	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
1155	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
1156	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
1157	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
1158	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
1159	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
1160	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
1161	other node event. Instance deletion and modification add their own
1162	`instance_deleted` and `instance_modified` events, and re-expansion adds a
1163	`map_reexpanded` event, described under
1164	"Delete and modify expanded instances" below.
1165	
1166	### Maps inside loop bodies
1167	
1168	A map node may belong to a loop body — it is part of the body exactly when
1169	the loop's entry or condition reaches it through `depends_on`, like any
1170	other body member:
1171	
1172	```json
1173	{"id": "fanout", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["attempt"],
1174	 "source": "attempt", "path": "items", "max_instances": 10,
1175	 "template": {"id": "work", "retries": 1}}
1176	```
1177	
1178	A nested map expands once per iteration, when every dependency of its node
1179	is completed or skipped in that iteration, and the element list is read from
1180	the source task's output of that same iteration. The expansion rules are the
1181	ones of an execution-level map: a missing path or a non-array value expands
1182	to zero instances and the map completes for that iteration with an empty
1183	output list, so the loop boundary is evaluated as usual; an element count
1184	beyond `max_instances` creates no instance at all — the map fails
1185	permanently, is listed under `failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates
1186	with reason `retries_exhausted` under the usual exhaustion semantics.
1187	
1188	The expanded instances belong to their iteration only: they queue in
1189	ascending element index order and are settled one per `advance`, exactly
1190	like execution-level instances, and one iteration's instances never
1191	overwrite another iteration's results. An instance is an ordinary task in
1192	every other respect — a submitted failure consumes the template's retry
1193	bound and re-queues that instance within its iteration, and a template
1194	approval point parks the execution until an approver decides it — with no
1195	influence from the iteration number.
1196	
1197	Iteration state exposes each nested map under the iteration record's `maps`
1198	field, with the same per-map shape as an execution-level map (`status`, one
1199	record per instance, the ordered completed `outputs`, and `failure_reason`);
1200	the field is present on every iteration of a loop whose body declares a map
1201	node. When a nested map completes, its node enters the iteration's
1202	`completed_nodes` and its output list is recorded in the iteration's
1203	`outputs`; when the loop finishes, the usual roll-up lists the map node once
1204	in the execution-level `completed_nodes`, while its outputs stay with their
1205	iterations. An execution-level `maps` field is not created for nested maps.
1206	
1207	Every event a nested expansion records carries the owning `loop_id` and
1208	`iteration` alongside the map id and, for per-instance events, the element
1209	`index`: `map_expanded`, `map_completed`, the per-instance `node_completed`,
1210	`node_failed`, and `node_retried`, and `approval_requested` and
1211	`approval_decided` for a template approval point. The `iteration_started`
1212	event of a loop whose body declares map nodes carries the iteration's
1213	initial `maps` skeleton, so replay rebuilds every iteration's instance list,
1214	status, and ownership solely from the event stream, consistent with the
1215	materialized state. Checkpoints are written at each iteration's instance
1216	boundaries, so recovery continues the current iteration's unfinished
1217	instances and never repeats an instance output. Cancellation, timeouts,
1218	leases, retries, and approvals keep their existing semantics, and a nested
1219	map never changes an execution's termination reason.
1220	
1221	Executions whose workflows declare no nested map behave exactly as before:
1222	state fields, event contents, and advancement results are unchanged.
1223	
1224	### Delete and modify expanded instances
1225	
1226	An expanded dynamic node offers, alongside expansion and per-instance
1227	advancement, two instance-level operations and a node-level re-expansion.
1228	All three are ordinary idempotent HTTP commands over the same entry points
1229	the rest of the service uses; they introduce no second protocol.
1230	
1231	An instance that has never advanced can be removed, and so can an instance
1232	that has permanently failed:
1233	
1234	```http
1235	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/2/delete
1236	Idempotency-Key: delete-instance-2
1237	
1238	{}
1239	```
1240	
1241	The body must be an empty object. Removing an instance drops only that
1242	instance's record: every retained instance keeps its element index, its
1243	place in the queue, and its advancement order. When the removed instance was
1244	the map's last unfinished instance, the node completes under the existing
1245	rules with an output list containing only the retained instances' outputs,
1246	in ascending element-index order, and its successors unlock as usual. An
1247	instance that is waiting on an approval, or has already completed, can never
1248	be deleted; attempting it returns `409 conflict` and changes no state. A
1249	permanently failed instance is removable after the execution has terminated,
1250	but removing it never revives the execution, alters its termination reason,
1251	or changes the node's failed conclusion. When every retained instance of a
1252	map inside a loop body has ended, the iteration's other nodes advance as
1253	usual and the node completes or ends under the existing rules; deleting an
1254	instance in one iteration never touches another iteration.
1255	
1256	An instance that has never advanced can also have its input rewritten
1257	before it is worked:
1258	
1259	```http
1260	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/1/modify
1261	Idempotency-Key: modify-instance-1
1262	
1263	{"input":{"address":"742 Evergreen Terrace"}}
1264	```
1265	
1266	The body must contain exactly `input`, an object with the new content; it is
1267	validated like every other request body (finite numbers only). The rewrite
1268	changes only the parameters used when that one instance is later advanced:
1269	it affects no other instance, and the output and history of an instance that
1270	has already advanced (waiting, completed, or permanently failed) are
1271	immutable — modifying such an instance returns `409 conflict` and changes no
1272	state. The rewritten input, including its full float precision and `-0.0`,
1273	is stored verbatim.
1274	
1275	Delete and modify calls on the same instance settle in call order: every
1276	call applies to the instance list exactly as the earlier calls left it, and
1277	several calls on one instance each take effect independently, one after
1278	another. A rewritten instance has still never advanced, so it remains
1279	deletable; deleting or modifying an instance an earlier call already
1280	removed is a `404 not_found`; and a second rewrite of the same instance
1281	records the first rewrite's content as its `before`.
1282	
1283	Both commands apply to a map nested in a loop body exactly as to an
1284	execution-level map: the current running iteration's instances are
1285	addressed by the same path, and every event they append carries the owning
1286	`loop_id` and `iteration` alongside the map id; an execution-level instance
1287	carries no loop context.
1288	
1289	An out-of-bounds element index, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic
1290	`map`, a missing execution, or a cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found`
1291	and writes nothing. A missing or mistyped field, a non-object modify
1292	`input`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a `400 validation_error`
1293	with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a
1294	`409 conflict`; repeating the same command with the same key returns the
1295	first result and appends no second event.
1296	
1297	Every successful call appends exactly one event to the execution stream:
1298	
1299	- an `instance_deleted` event records the action type, the owning dynamic
1300	  node under `map_id`, the removed instance's element `index` and `status`
1301	  (`ready` or `failed`), and, for a map inside a loop body, the `loop_id`
1302	  and `iteration`;
1303	- an `instance_modified` event records the action type, the owning
1304	  `map_id`, the instance `index`, the content `before` the rewrite (`null`
1305	  for an instance that had never been rewritten) and `after` it, and the
1306	  same loop context when the instance belongs to an iteration.
1307	
1308	Replay rebuilds the instance list, every instance's status and ownership,
1309	and each rewrite solely from the event stream: a delete drops the recorded
1310	instance (and the subsequent `map_completed`, when the deletion finished the
1311	node, completes it with the retained outputs), and a modify applies the
1312	rewritten input to that one instance, so the rebuilt state is exactly the
1313	materialized state. A checkpoint is written at the instance boundary of
1314	every successful delete or modify; after a restart recovery continues the
1315	unfinished instances, repeats no instance output, and never resurrects a
1316	deleted instance. The operations change no advancement conclusion or
1317	termination semantics: cancellation, timeouts, approvals, leases, retries,
1318	and retry exhaustion keep their existing behavior. Executions that never
1319	use deletion, modification, or re-expansion keep exactly their current
1320	state fields, event contents, and advancement results.
1321	
1322	### Re-expand a dynamic node
1323	
1324	A dynamic node that has already expanded can be expanded again on demand —
1325	above all to regenerate its instance list after deletions:
1326	
1327	```http
1328	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/reexpand
1329	Idempotency-Key: reexpand-1
1330	
1331	{}
1332	```
1333	
1334	(The same operation is also accepted at `.../maps/ship/expand`.) The body
1335	must be an empty object. Re-expansion reads the element list again from the
1336	source task's recorded output — the same recorded output the first
1337	expansion read, which never changes once recorded — and regenerates the
1338	instance list from it: every previous instance record is replaced, and the
1339	fresh instances queue from element index zero in ascending order. The
1340	regenerated instances are ordinary instances in every respect: they are
1341	deleted, modified, advanced, retried, and approved through the same entries
1342	and with exactly the same behavior as a first expansion, and their retry
1343	bounds start from zero.
1344	
1345	Every successful call appends exactly one `map_reexpanded` event, recording
1346	the action type, the owning dynamic node under `map_id`, and the number of
1347	generated instances under `instance_count`; for a map inside a loop body
1348	the event also carries the owning `loop_id` and `iteration`, and only the
1349	current running iteration's expansion is replaced. A node that had
1350	completed returns to `running`: it leaves `completed_nodes`, its recorded
1351	output entry is discarded, and when the regenerated instances have all
1352	completed the node completes again under the existing rules, its result
1353	list holding only the finally retained instances' outputs in ascending
1354	element-index order. An empty element list completes the node again at
1355	once with an empty output list, exactly like a zero-element first
1356	expansion.
1357	
1358	Re-expansion is rejected with `409 conflict` and writes nothing when the
1359	node has not expanded yet, when it has permanently failed, when one of its
1360	instances is waiting on an approval decision, when the execution has
1361	already completed, or when a nested map's loop is not currently running.
1362	A terminated execution's unfinished node may still be re-expanded; doing so
1363	never revives the execution or alters its termination reason. A missing
1364	execution, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic `map`, or a
1365	cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found` and writes nothing. A
1366	non-empty or non-object body, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
1367	`400 validation_error` with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key
1368	from another operation is a `409 conflict`; repeating the same call with
1369	the same key returns the first result and appends no second event. Replay
1370	rebuilds the regenerated instance list, statuses, and ownership solely
1371	from the event stream, a checkpoint is written at the re-expansion
1372	boundary, and recovery after a restart continues the unfinished
1373	regenerated instances — repeating no instance output and never resurrecting
1374	an instance that stayed deleted.
1375	
1376	### Workflow versions
1377	
1378	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
1379	
1380	```json
1381	{
1382	  "id": "order-flow",
1383	  "version": "2026-09-25",
1384	  "nodes": [
1385	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
1386	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
1387	  ]
1388	}
1389	```
1390	
1391	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
1392	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
1393	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
1394	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
1395	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
1396	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
1397	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
1398	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
1399	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
