1554	### List workflows
1555	
1556	```http
1557	GET /workflows?limit=50
1558	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1559	```
1560	
1561	Enumerates the workflows declared in the request's namespace. The response
1562	is `{"workflows":[{"id":"order-flow"}, ...]}`: one entry per workflow, each
1563	carrying its identifier, in ascending identifier order. A namespace with no
1564	workflows gets the definite empty result `{"workflows":[]}`, not an error.
1565	The query is read-only: it creates nothing, appends no events, and records
1566	no usage, so repeating it returns the same answer and changes no stored
1567	state.
1568	
1569	The list is paged with a keyset cursor:
1570	
1571	- `limit` — required; the maximum number of entries in the page, a positive
1572	  integer. The page never holds more entries than the limit;
1573	- `cursor` — optional; the identifier of the previous page's last entry.
1574	  Only entries whose identifier sorts strictly after the cursor are
1575	  returned, so paging with the previous page's last identifier yields
1576	  consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A cursor past the end
1577	  returns the definite empty list.
1578	
1579	### List executions
1580	
1581	```http
1582	GET /executions?workflow_id=order-flow&status=terminated&termination_reason=timeout&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=run-41&limit=50
1583	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1584	```
1585	
1586	Enumerates the executions in the request's namespace in ascending execution
1587	identifier order. The response is `{"executions":[...]}`; each entry carries
1588	the execution `id`, its `workflow_id`, its `status` (`running`, `completed`,
1589	or `terminated`, always a string), its `termination_reason` (one of the
1590	four termination reasons for a terminated execution, otherwise `null`), and
1591	its `created_at` (the ISO-8601 UTC creation timestamp ending in `Z`), in
1592	that stable key order. A namespace with no executions gets the definite
1593	empty result `{"executions":[]}`. Like the workflows list this query is
1594	read-only and never settles a due timeout, appends an event, writes a
1595	checkpoint, or records usage, so repeated calls return the same answer and
1596	change no state or metering conclusion.
1597	
1598	The same `limit` and `cursor` pagination applies, with the cursor taken
1599	from the previous page's last execution identifier. In addition, five
1600	filters may be combined, and every given filter must match:
1601	
1602	- `workflow_id` — only executions of that workflow. Referencing a workflow
1603	  the namespace does not contain, including one owned by another tenant, is
1604	  the usual `404 not_found` and reveals nothing about its existence;
1605	- `status` — only executions in that lifecycle status. A value other than
1606	  `running`, `completed`, or `terminated` is a `400 validation_error`;
1607	- `termination_reason` — only executions that terminated for exactly that
1608	  reason. The filter is meaningful solely for terminated executions:
1609	  running and completed executions never appear under it, even when other
1610	  filters are given alongside it. An unknown reason is a
1611	  `400 validation_error`;
1612	- `since` and `until` — the same closed creation-time bounds the events and
1613	  metrics queries accept: each is an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp ending in `Z`,
1614	  and an execution whose `created_at` equals `since` or `until` is
1615	  returned. When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is
1616	  open, so omitting both returns exactly the unfiltered list; a malformed
1617	  timestamp is a `400 validation_error`. When `since` is later than
1618	  `until` the window matches nothing and the result is the definite empty
1619	  list, not an error.
1620	
1621	Both list endpoints follow the usual tenant scope: omitting
1622	`X-Tenant-Id` keeps the single legacy namespace, and a tenant sees only its
1623	own workflows and executions under every combination of filters. Every
1624	parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1625	parameter, a missing `limit`, or a `limit` that is not a positive integer is
1626	a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing.

1628	### Inspect an execution
1629	
1630	```http
1631	GET /executions/run-1
1632	GET /executions/run-1/events
1633	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
1634	```
1635	
1636	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
1637	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
1638	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
1639	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
1640	
1641	The events query is read-only: it appends no events, records no usage, and
1642	changes no state, so advancement, approvals, recovery, and replay never alter
1643	what it observes. With no query parameters it returns the complete ordered
1644	event list exactly as before. It also accepts optional filter and pagination
1645	parameters, which combine as an intersection:
1646	
1647	```http
1648	GET /executions/run-1/events?types=node_completed,node_failed&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
1649	```
1650	
1651	- `types` — a comma-separated set of event types; only events whose type is
1652	  in the set are returned. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown
1653	  event type is a `400 validation_error`;
1654	- `since` and `until` — the same closed-interval occurrence-time bounds the
1655	  metrics query accepts: an event whose time equals either boundary is
1656	  returned. When `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing and
1657	  the result is an empty list, not an error;
1658	- `cursor` — the sequence of the last event of the previous page; only events
1659	  with a strictly greater sequence are returned;
1660	- `limit` — the maximum number of events in the page, in ascending sequence
1661	  order.
1662	
1663	Every parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1664	parameter, a malformed timestamp, or a cursor or limit that is not a positive
1665	integer is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Filtering never
1666	renumbers events, so paging with `cursor` set to the previous page's last
1667	sequence yields consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A filter
1668	that matches nothing returns the definite empty result `{"events":[]}`, and
1669	querying a missing or another tenant's execution is the usual
1670	`404 not_found`.

1672	### Webhook notifications
1673	
1674	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
1675	messages when business events occur. Each webhook subscription contains exactly:
1676	
1677	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
1678	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
1679	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
1680	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
1681	  reason);
1682	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
1683	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
1684	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
1685	
1686	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
1687	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1688	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
1689	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
1690	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written. A subscription
1691	may instead declare a queue target (`queue` instead of `url`); see "Queue
1692	subscriptions" below.
1693	
1694	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
1695	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
1696	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
1697	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
1698	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
1699	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
1700	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
1701	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
1702	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
1703	triggered it.
1704	
1705	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
1706	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
1707	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
1708	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
1709	results as before.
1710	
1711	### Inspect the delivery history
1712	
1713	```http
1714	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
1715	```
1716	
1717	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
1718	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
1719	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
1720	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
1721	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
1722	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
1723	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
1724	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
1725	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
1726	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
1727	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
1728	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
1729	
1730	### Queue subscriptions
1731	
1732	A subscription may declare a queue target instead of a webhook `url`:
1733	
1734	```json
1735	{
1736	  "id": "run-4",
1737	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1738	  "input": {},
1739	  "subscriptions": [{"queue": "order-events", "events": ["node_completed"], "visibility_seconds": 60}]
1740	}
1741	```
1742	
1743	A queue subscription contains exactly:
1744	
1745	- `queue`: a non-empty queue name of any length;
1746	- `events`: the same non-empty event-type list a webhook subscription takes;
1747	- `visibility_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds a pulled
1748	  message stays invisible while awaiting acknowledgement, defaulting to 30.
1749	
1750	Exactly one of `url` and `queue` must be present in a subscription. Any
1751	other field, a missing or invalid `events` list, an empty queue name, or a
1752	non-positive or non-finite visibility timeout is a 400 `validation_error`
1753	that rejects the whole request without partial writes. Queue names are
1754	unique per tenant across declarations: declaring a name that another
1755	workflow or execution of the same tenant already declared is a 409
1756	`conflict`, while different tenants may reuse the same names freely.
1757	
1758	A workflow or an execution may declare several queue targets. Every
1759	execution gets its own queues — those declared on the workflow revision it
1760	is bound to, plus those it declares itself — and when a subscribed event
1761	occurs, a message carrying the event type and its details is appended to
1762	each matching queue of that execution, in occurrence order. The append is
1763	atomic with the event itself: a rejected operation leaves no queued message
1764	behind. Each message carries an idempotency key that is deterministic per
1765	event and queue: every delivery of the same message reuses the same key,
1766	and different events never share a key. Queues add no fields to the
1767	execution state and append no events, and replay, recovery, and queries
1768	never enqueue. Executions that declare no queue targets behave exactly as
1769	before.
1770	
1771	### Inspect the queue state
1772	
1773	```http
1774	GET /executions/run-4/queues
1775	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1776	```
1777	
1778	Returns `{"queues": [...]}` with one entry per queue of the execution, in
1779	declaration order; an execution with no queue targets gets the definite
1780	empty result `{"queues": []}`. Each entry gives its `queue` name, the
1781	`visibility_seconds` in effect, and the queue's `messages` in entry order —
1782	an empty list for a queue that never received a message. Each message record
1783	gives its `sequence` (the entry order), the `event_type` and
1784	`event_sequence` that produced it, the event `payload`, the message
1785	`idempotency_key`, the `delivery_count`, a `deliveries` list recording every
1786	delivery with its `delivery` number and `delivered_at` time, the
1787	`enqueued_at` time, and the current `status` (`pending`, `delivered`, or
1788	`acknowledged`). Querying the queues of a missing execution — including one
1789	owned by another tenant — is the usual 404 `not_found`.
1790	
1791	### Pull messages from a queue
1792	
1793	```http
1794	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/pull
1795	Idempotency-Key: pull-request-1
1796	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1797	
1798	{}
1799	```
1800	
1801	The body must be an empty object. The response is `{"messages": [...]}`: the
1802	currently pending messages in entry order, each rendered like the message
1803	records of the queue state query. A pulled message becomes invisible for the
1804	queue's visibility timeout; if it is not acknowledged by then, it returns to
1805	the pending set and is delivered again — the queue semantics are at least
1806	once, and every delivery is recorded in the message's delivery history.
1807	Pulling an empty queue, or one whose messages are all invisible, is a
1808	definite empty result `{"messages": []}`, not an error. Every delivery to
1809	the caller is metered as one `delivery_attempted` usage record, exactly like
1810	an outbound webhook attempt, and counts toward the tenant's bill.
1811	
1812	### Acknowledge a message
1813	
1814	```http
1815	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/ack
1816	Idempotency-Key: ack-request-1
1817	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1818	
1819	{"idempotency_key": "run-4:2:queue:order-events"}
1820	```
1821	
1822	The body must contain exactly `idempotency_key`, naming a message of the
1823	queue. Acknowledgement is explicit and final: the message permanently leaves
1824	the queue and is never delivered again, and the response is
1825	`{"acknowledged": true}`. Acknowledging a message that was already
1826	acknowledged, or a key the queue does not know, is a 404 `not_found`.
1827	Pulling from or acknowledging a queue the execution does not have, or one
1828	belonging to a missing or cross-tenant execution, is likewise a 404
1829	`not_found`. Pull and acknowledge are idempotent commands like every other
1830	operation: repeating one with the same `Idempotency-Key` returns the
1831	original result, and reusing a key across different operations is a 409
1832	`conflict`.
1833	
1834	### Schedules
1835	
1836	A workflow may declare a schedule so the service creates executions
1837	automatically. The declaration happens at workflow creation (a `schedule`
1838	field next to `id` and `nodes`) or later through the update endpoint, and it
1839	takes effect from the moment it is stored. A schedule contains exactly:
1840	
1841	- `interval_seconds`: a positive integer number of seconds between runs —
1842	  or, alternatively, `cron`: a five-field cron expression (`minute hour
1843	  day-of-month month day-of-week`) whose fields support `*`, `*/step`,
1844	  single values, ranges `a-b`, ranges with steps `a-b/step`, and
1845	  comma-separated lists, with 0 and 7 both meaning Sunday. Exactly one of
1846	  `interval_seconds` and `cron` must be present;
1847	- `input`: the object used as the execution input of every created run;
1848	- `missed_policy`: either `catch_up` or `skip`.
1849	
1850	Whenever a period of the plan comes due, the service creates one execution
1851	for the workflow with the declared input. The created execution is exactly a
1852	manually created one: it starts `running` with the same state shape and the
1853	usual `execution_started` event, and advancing, approvals, leases, retries,
1854	timeouts, and cancellation all behave identically. The trigger itself writes
1855	nothing into the created execution's event stream and adds no fields to its
1856	state; the schedule's own record of when it fired and which execution it
1857	created is exposed through the status query below.
1858	
1859	Creation is idempotent per schedule period: a repeated trigger or a repeated
1860	request for the same period returns the same execution and never creates a
1861	second one, under either missed policy. When periods were missed — the
1862	schedule was paused, or the service was not running — `catch_up` makes up
1863	exactly the single most recent missed period, while `skip` makes up none;
1864	neither policy ever creates more than one execution for the same period.
1865	
1866	An invalid declaration rejects the whole request with 400
1867	`validation_error` and writes nothing: a non-positive or non-integer
1868	`interval_seconds`, a cron expression with other than five fields, out-of
1869	range values, or unparseable fragments, declaring both `interval_seconds`
1870	and `cron`, a `missed_policy` other than `catch_up` or `skip`, a missing or
1871	mistyped `input`, or any unknown field.
1872	
1873	### Declare or replace a schedule
1874	
1875	```http
1876	PUT /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
1877	Idempotency-Key: schedule-request-1
1878	
1879	{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"}
1880	```
1881	
1882	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body is validated exactly
1883	like a schedule declared at creation time, and the response is the schedule
1884	status. Updating replaces the plan and re-anchors it at the update time; the
1885	paused flag is kept. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`, an invalid
1886	plan 400 `validation_error` with no partial write, and reusing an
1887	idempotency key from another operation is a 409 `conflict`.
1888	
1889	### Inspect the schedule status
1890	
1891	```http
1892	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule
1893	```
1894	
1895	Returns a single `schedule` object with the status fields, or the definite
1896	empty result `{"schedule":null}` for a workflow that never declared a
1897	schedule. When a schedule exists the object is:
1898	
1899	```json
1900	{
1901	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"},
1902	  "paused": false,
1903	  "last_triggered_at": "2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z",
1904	  "last_execution_id": "nightly-orders-scheduled-i:42"
1905	}
1906	```
1907	
1908	The fields are:
1909	
1910	- `schedule`: the declared plan exactly as stored — either
1911	  `{"interval_seconds": <positive integer>, "input": <object>, "missed_policy": "catch_up"|"skip"}`
1912	  or `{"cron": "<five-field expression>", "input": <object>, "missed_policy": ...}`;
1913	  the input is the declared object verbatim;
1914	- `paused`: a JSON boolean;
1915	- `last_triggered_at`: an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp string ending in `Z`, or
1916	  `null` until the first period fires;
1917	- `last_execution_id`: the execution id string of the most recently created
1918	  run, or `null` until the first trigger.
1919	
1920	`last_triggered_at` and `last_execution_id` are `null` (not omitted) until
1921	the first trigger. A missing workflow returns 404 `not_found`.
1922	
1923	### Preview upcoming triggers
1924	
1925	```http
1926	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/preview?limit=3
1927	```
1928	
1929	Returns the trigger times the declared plan would settle next, starting
1930	from the first period that has not been settled yet, together with the
1931	input each created execution would carry:
1932	
1933	```json
1934	{
1935	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"},
1936	  "previews": [
1937	    {"trigger_at": "2026-09-27T09:00:00.000000Z", "input": {"mode": "nightly"}},
1938	    {"trigger_at": "2026-09-27T10:00:00.000000Z", "input": {"mode": "nightly"}},
1939	    {"trigger_at": "2026-09-27T11:00:00.000000Z", "input": {"mode": "nightly"}}
1940	  ]
1941	}
1942	```
1943	
1944	- `schedule`: the declared plan exactly as stored, like the status query;
1945	- `previews`: up to `limit` entries in ascending time order, each carrying
1946	  `trigger_at` (an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp string ending in `Z`) and `input`
1947	  (the declared input object verbatim).
1948	
1949	A fixed interval projects continuously from the next unsettled period; a
1950	cron plan takes the next minute matching its field rules, then the one
1951	after that, and so on. The `limit` query parameter is required, must be a
1952	positive integer, and may appear at most once; a missing, repeated, or
1953	malformed value — or any other query parameter — is a 400
1954	`validation_error`. The preview is read-only: it creates no execution,
1955	appends no event, and never moves the schedule's cursor, so repeating the
1956	query returns the same projection. A paused schedule projects exactly like
1957	a running one — the missed policy only governs whether a due period
1958	creates an execution, never the projection. A workflow that never declared
1959	a schedule returns the definite empty result `{"schedule":null}`, exactly
1960	like the status query; a missing or cross-tenant workflow returns 404
1961	`not_found`.
1962	
1963	### Pause and resume a schedule
1964	
1965	```http
1966	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/pause
1967	Idempotency-Key: pause-request-1
1968	
1969	{}
1970	```
1971	
1972	```http
1973	POST /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/resume
1974	Idempotency-Key: resume-request-1
1975	
1976	{}
1977	```
1978	
1979	Both bodies must be empty objects; a missing or mistyped body, an unknown
1980	field, or a non-finite number is a 400 `validation_error`. While paused, due
1981	periods create no executions. Resuming settles the periods that came due
1982	during the pause according to the missed policy: `catch_up` immediately
1983	creates the single most recent missed run, `skip` creates none. Pausing or
1984	resuming a workflow that has no schedule, or any schedule operation on a
1985	missing workflow, returns 404 `not_found`; reusing an idempotency key across
1986	operations returns 409 `conflict`. Both responses carry the schedule status.
1987	
1988	Workflows that declare no schedule are unaffected: their creation,
1989	advancement, approvals, deliveries, checkpoints, recovery, and replay behave
1990	exactly as before, with no additional fields or events.
1991	
1992	### Schedule change history
1993	
1994	Every successful schedule declaration, replacement, pause, and resume leaves
1995	one change record, so a caller can see exactly when each scheduling change
1996	took effect; every other operation — reads, previews, and the automatic
1997	triggering of due periods included — leaves no record. The history hangs off
1998	the same schedule entry point the status and preview use, with the same
1999	calling shape as the price-table change history:
2000	
2001	```http
2002	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/history?limit=50
2003	X-Tenant-Id: acme
2004	```
2005	
2006	Returns `{"history":[...]}` with the records in ascending order of occurrence
2007	time; records sharing one instant are ordered by a stable ascending sequence.
2008	Each record is:
2009	
2010	```json
2011	{"sequence":7,"action":"declare","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z","snapshot":{"schedule":{"interval_seconds":3600,"input":{"mode":"nightly"},"missed_policy":"catch_up"},"paused":false}}
2012	```
2013	
2014	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant and
2015	  workflow, shared across every kind of schedule change. It identifies the
2016	  record across every query and is never renumbered by a filter or a page;
2017	- `action` is `declare` for a schedule declaration or a replacement (including
2018	  one carried by workflow creation or an added version), `pause` for a pause,
2019	  or `resume` for a resume;
2020	- `occurred_at` is the moment the change took effect, an ISO-8601 UTC string
2021	  ending in `Z`;
2022	- `snapshot` is the complete schedule in effect after the change, listing
2023	  `schedule` — the declared plan exactly as stored, the plan text preserved
2024	  verbatim and never rewritten (a cron expression stays its original
2025	  five-field text, and the input keeps its original content) — followed by
2026	  `paused`, the pause flag then in effect. A declaration or replacement keeps
2027	  the previous pause flag, so a replacement made while paused snapshots
2028	  `"paused":true`; a pause snapshots `true` and a resume `false`.
2029	
2030	The history record is written atomically with the change it describes, in the
2031	same transaction as the schedule write, so a reader always sees the schedule
2032	and its history agree. A declaration rejected by validation, a pause or resume
2033	of a missing workflow or one without a schedule, an idempotency-key conflict,
2034	or a key reused for another operation leaves no record. Repeating the same
2035	declaration, replacement, pause, or resume with the same key returns the first
2036	result, byte for byte, and appends no second record; reusing a key for another
2037	operation is the usual `409 conflict` and, again, writes no history.
2038	
2039	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
2040	`{"history":[]}`, never an error. The response is one line of compact JSON
2041	with the record keys in the order above, full number precision preserved
2042	(including `-0.0`), and a single trailing newline, like every other JSON
2043	endpoint.
2044	
2045	The endpoint accepts an optional action filter, the same optional closed time
2046	window the per-record usage query accepts, plus cursor pagination, in exactly
2047	the same shape as the price-table change history:
2048	
2049	```http
2050	GET /workflows/nightly-orders/schedule/history?action=declare,pause,resume&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
2051	```
2052	
2053	- `action` names one action or a comma-separated set of them (`declare`,
2054	  `pause`, and `resume`); only records whose action is in the set are
2055	  returned. A single value needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry,
2056	  or an unknown action is a `400 validation_error`; when `action` is absent
2057	  every change is returned;
2058	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
2059	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
2060	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
2061	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing
2062	  and the definite empty list is returned;
2063	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
2064	  contains more than that many records;
2065	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
2066	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
2067	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
2068	- the action filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
2069	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
2070	
2071	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `action` entry, a
2072	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
2073	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
2074	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
2075	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. Querying the history of a
2076	missing workflow, or of a workflow owned by another tenant, is answered
2077	exactly like a missing workflow: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the
2078	workflow exists elsewhere; another tenant's records are never visible under
2079	any action filter, window, or page. The query is read-only: it appends no
2080	history, writes no metering record, settles no due period, and changes no
2081	schedule declaration, trigger cursor, usage, bill, quota, approval, or replay
2082	conclusion. The history entry point changes no existing behavior: declaring or
2083	replacing a schedule, pausing and resuming it, and the automatic triggering of
2084	due periods are byte-for-byte unchanged apart from the additional history row
2085	the successful write now commits.
2086	
2087	### Checkpoints
2088	
2089	Every successful `advance` that settles a node boundary — a task is
2090	completed, or a failure is submitted (whether it retries or exhausts the
2091	attempts) — writes a checkpoint in the same transaction as the state update
2092	and event append. The checkpoint stores the complete state summary at that
2093	boundary, including completed, skipped, and failed nodes, condition results,
2094	outputs, attempts with their unfinished retry counts, and the status and
2095	current iteration of every loop (with the per-iteration records), together
2096	with the position of the last written event. Because the checkpoint matches
2097	the stored state at that position, recovery can continue without replaying or
2098	duplicating any node output.
2099	
2100	Checkpoints do not add fields to the execution state and do not append events:
2101	an execution that declares no retries, timeout, or loops keeps exactly the
2102	same state shape and event stream as before.
2103	
2104	### Complete the next ready node
2105	
2106	```http
2107	POST /executions/run-1/advance
2108	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-1
2109	
2110	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"}}
2111	```
2112	
2113	The lexicographically first ready task is completed. The response contains the
2114	updated execution. Before that, each call first evaluates all ready conditions
2115	in deterministic order and skips tasks whose `run_if` does not match; if this
2116	automatic processing finishes the execution, the current state is returned and
2117	the submitted output is not consumed. When every node is completed or skipped,
2118	the status becomes `completed`.
2119	
2120	Instead of an output, a failure can be submitted for the same ready task:
2121	
2122	```http
2123	POST /executions/run-1/advance
2124	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-2
2125	
2126	{"failure":{"reason":"gateway timeout"}}
2127	```
2128	
2129	The body must contain exactly one of `output` or `failure`, and `failure`
2130	carries exactly a `reason` string. Either body may additionally carry a
2131	`worker_id` string identifying the lease holder when the execution's work
2132	item has been claimed (see "Claim a work item"). A failed task appends a `node_failed`
2133	event recording the attempt number and reason. While the task has retries
2134	left it returns to the ready set and a `node_retried` event records the next
2135	attempt number; otherwise the task is permanently failed and the execution
2136	terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`. The same rules apply to tasks
2137	inside loop bodies, which are retried within their current iteration.
2138	
2139	Execution state includes `completed_nodes` (which also lists evaluated
2140	conditions), `skipped_nodes`, `failed_nodes`, `condition_results`, `outputs`,
2141	and `attempts`. `attempts` maps each attempted task to its current `attempt`
2142	number and its `failures` count; loop body tasks track the same per iteration.
2143	Executions of workflows that declare approval points additionally expose
2144	`waiting_approval` (`null`, or the pending point's `node_id`, `approvers`, and
2145	loop context) and the `approvals` record list. Each condition evaluation
2146	appends a `condition_evaluated` event and each skip a `node_skipped` event to
2147	the execution stream.
2148	
2149	### Cancel an execution
2150	
2151	```http
2152	POST /executions/run-1/cancel
2153	Idempotency-Key: cancel-request-1
2154	```
2155	
2156	A running execution is terminated immediately with termination reason
2157	`cancelled`. Cancelling a completed or already terminated execution returns
2158	its state unchanged, and cancelling a missing execution returns 404.
2159	
2160	Execution status is `running`, `completed`, or `terminated`. A terminated
2161	execution records exactly one `termination_reason` — `retries_exhausted`,
2162	`rejected`, `timeout`, or `cancelled` — and appends a single
2163	`execution_terminated` event; completed executions keep a `null` termination
2164	reason and their own `execution_completed` event. Advancing a terminated
2165	execution returns its state unchanged without consuming the submitted output
2166	or failure; a decision against one only succeeds as a repeat of the decision
2167	that rejected it, and otherwise conflicts.
2168	
2169	### Claim a work item
2170	
2171	```http
2172	POST /executions/run-1/claim
2173	Idempotency-Key: claim-request-1
2174	
2175	{"worker_id":"worker-7","lease_seconds":30}
2176	```
2177	
2178	Claiming is how an external worker takes ownership of a running execution
2179	before advancing its ready tasks. `worker_id` is a non-empty string and
2180	`lease_seconds` is an optional positive number of seconds (default 30). The
2181	response contains the claimed `work_item` (its `execution_id` and
2182	`workflow_id`) and a `lease` recording the `worker_id`, the `lease_seconds`
2183	duration, the `expires_at` deadline, and the `heartbeat_at` active time.
2184	Each work item is held by at most one worker at a time: claiming a work
2185	item whose lease is still active — even by the same worker — is a 409
2186	`conflict`. Claiming a completed or terminated execution returns the
2187	definite empty result `{"work_item":null,"lease":null}` and absorbs no
2188	input, and claiming a missing execution returns 404.
2189	
2190	While a work item is held, results are submitted through the usual
2191	`advance` entry by including the holder's identity:
2192	
2193	```http
2194	POST /executions/run-1/advance
2195	Idempotency-Key: advance-request-3
2196	
2197	{"output":{"reservation_id":"r-9"},"worker_id":"worker-7"}
2198	```
2199	
2200	Submitting results for a work item held by another worker, or after the
2201	lease has expired, is a 409 `conflict` that does not change execution
2202	state. An execution that never claimed a work item accepts `advance`
2203	exactly as before, and its state fields and event stream are identical to
2204	an execution without any claim.
2205	
2206	When a lease expires, the work item returns to the claimable set and may be
2207	claimed again by the same or another worker. The second claim continues
2208	from the materialized state: node outputs and results recorded by the
2209	earlier holder are never advanced or recorded twice, and every written
2210	output belongs to the single advance that submitted it.
2211	
2212	### Renew a lease
2213	
2214	```http
2215	POST /executions/run-1/heartbeat
2216	Idempotency-Key: heartbeat-request-1
2217	
2218	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
2219	```
2220	
2221	Within the lease period the holder may heartbeat to extend `expires_at` by
2222	the lease duration and refresh the `heartbeat_at` active time; the response
2223	carries the updated `lease`. A heartbeat never advances nodes, writes
2224	outputs, or appends node events. A heartbeat from another worker or after
2225	the lease expired is a 409 `conflict`; a heartbeat for a missing execution
2226	or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404 `not_found`.
2227	
2228	### Release a work item
2229	
2230	```http
2231	POST /executions/run-1/release
2232	Idempotency-Key: release-request-1
2233	
2234	{"worker_id":"worker-7"}
2235	```
2236	
2237	Releasing invalidates the lease immediately and returns the work item to
2238	the claimable set, so it can be claimed again right away; progress already
2239	made and the recorded events are unchanged. Releasing with another
2240	worker's identity or after expiry is a 409 `conflict`; releasing for a
2241	missing execution or an execution with no claimed work item is a 404
2242	`not_found`.
2243	
2244	Claims, heartbeats, and releases append no events and add no fields to the
2245	execution state, so replay, checkpoints, and recovery are unaffected.
2246	Leases live in the same SQLite database as the execution state, so
2247	unexpired leases and claim ownership remain valid after the service
2248	restarts.
2249	
2250	### Recover from a checkpoint
2251	
2252	```http
2253	POST /executions/run-1/recover
2254	Idempotency-Key: recover-request-1
2255	
2256	{"from":"latest_checkpoint"}
2257	```
2258	
2259	Recovery rebuilds a running execution from its latest checkpoint and returns
2260	the rebuilt execution. It appends no events and changes no state: the rebuilt
2261	execution is exactly the materialized state, and a subsequent replay has the
2262	same conclusion as before the interruption. After recovery, further
2263	`advance` calls continue from the checkpoint, so node outputs, failure
2264	reasons, attempt numbers, and loop iteration ownership are identical to an
2265	uninterrupted run; failure records for tasks inside a loop body still carry
2266	their loop id and current iteration. Recovery works after the service has
2267	been restarted, because checkpoints live in the same SQLite database as the
2268	execution state and events.
2269	
2270	A completed execution is returned unchanged, producing no new events. A
2271	terminated execution is likewise returned unchanged and the operation
2272	absorbs no input; if a timeout or cancellation takes effect between
2273	checkpoint writes, termination takes precedence over recovery. Events and
2274	checkpoints remain queryable after cancellation or timeout, and their replay
2275	stays consistent with the materialized state.
2276	
2277	Recovering a missing execution returns 404. Recovering an execution that has
2278	no checkpoint, or whose latest checkpoint cannot be parsed, returns 409
2279	`conflict`. A missing `from` field, a wrong type, or an unknown recovery
2280	origin is a 400 `validation_error`; a non-finite number in the body is
2281	rejected the same way as every other request. Reusing an idempotency key
2282	already used by another operation (including an `advance` or `cancel` on the
2283	same execution) returns 409 `conflict`.
2284	
2285	### Replay
2286	
2287	```http
2288	POST /executions/run-1/replay
2289	```
2290	
2291	Rebuilds state solely from the execution event stream and compares it with the
2292	stored materialized state. A successful response contains `consistent: true`
2293	and the rebuilt execution.
2294	
2295	## Errors
2296	
2297	Errors use this shape:
2298	
2299	```json
2300	{"error":{"code":"validation_error","message":"human readable detail"}}
2301	```
2302	
2303	Validation errors return 400, missing resources return 404, and conflicts
2304	return 409. An empty `X-Tenant-Id` header value is a validation error; quota
2305	declarations and deletes and both quota reads, price declarations and price deletes, and the usage, bill,
2306	and metrics queries require a tenant, and quota limits and declared unit
2307	prices are positive integers validated by the
2308	same rules as every other body (no non-finite numbers, no unknown fields).
2309	Reusing a workflow or execution identifier, adding a workflow version whose
2310	tag already exists for that workflow, or reusing an idempotency key across
2311	different operations (within the same tenant), is a conflict. Starting an
2312	execution against a missing workflow or a missing workflow version is a
2313	missing resource (`404 not_found`). Migrating an execution to a missing
2314	version is likewise a missing resource, while migrating a completed or
2315	terminated execution is a conflict; a malformed migration body is a
2316	validation error, and a migration to the version already bound is a
2317	state-returning no-op rather than an error.
2318	Exceeding a tenant's declared workflow or execution quota is also a `409
2319	conflict`, with the word "quota" in the message so it can be distinguished
2320	from an identifier conflict; the rejected request writes nothing. Referencing
2321	a resource owned by another tenant is a missing resource (`404
2322	not_found`), indistinguishable from one that does not exist, so existence is
2323	never revealed across tenants. A `retries` value that is negative, non-integer, or greater than
2324	10, and a non-positive `timeout_seconds`, are validation errors. A malformed
2325	subscription — a missing or mistyped field, an unknown field, an empty or
2326	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
2327	a non-positive timeout or attempt count, more than ten attempts, a
2328	subscription declaring both `url` and `queue` or neither, an empty queue
2329	name, or a non-positive visibility timeout — is a
2330	validation error that rejects the whole request without partial writes, and
2331	querying the delivery history or the queues of a missing execution is a
2332	missing resource. Declaring a queue name another workflow or execution of
2333	the same tenant already declared is a conflict. Pulling from or
2334	acknowledging a missing queue, and acknowledging an unknown or already
2335	acknowledged message, are missing resources; a pull body that is not an
2336	empty object, or an acknowledgement body without exactly an
2337	`idempotency_key` string, is a validation error. An approval
2338	point with an empty approver list, a duplicate or non-string approver, an
2339	approval on a non-task node, and a decision body that is malformed or carries
2340	a decision other than `approved` or `rejected` are validation errors.
2341	A map node with an unknown or missing field, a mistyped or non-positive
2342	`max_instances`, an invalid template, a `source` that is not a
2343	task dependency, or an invalid `path` is likewise a validation error that
2344	rejects the whole request, whether the map stands alone or sits inside a
2345	loop body.
2346	Deleting or modifying an expanded instance whose index is out of bounds,
2347	whose map node does not exist, whose execution is missing, or that belongs
2348	to another tenant is a missing resource; deleting an instance that is
2349	waiting on an approval or already completed, or modifying any instance that
2350	has already advanced, is a conflict; a delete body that is not empty, a
2351	modify body without exactly an `input` object, and any unknown field or
2352	non-finite number are validation errors that write nothing.
2353	Re-expanding a node that is not a dynamic `map`, a missing execution, or a
2354	cross-tenant reference is likewise a missing resource; re-expanding a node
2355	that has not expanded yet, has permanently failed, has an instance waiting
2356	on an approval, belongs to a completed execution, or sits in a loop that is
2357	not currently running is a conflict; a re-expansion body that is not an
2358	empty object is a validation error that writes nothing.
2359	A decision by an approver who is
2360	not listed for the pending point, or any decision against an execution that
2361	has no pending approval point (other than a repeat of the decision that
2362	resolved the latest one), is a conflict. Claiming a work item whose lease is
2363	still active, submitting results for a work item held by another worker or
2364	after the lease expired, and heartbeating or releasing a lease held by
2365	another worker are conflicts, while heartbeating or releasing an execution
2366	with no claimed work item is a missing resource. Recovering a missing
2367	execution is a missing resource, while recovering an execution that has no
2368	checkpoint or whose latest checkpoint is unparseable is a conflict; an
2369	invalid recover body is a validation error. An invalid schedule declaration —
2370	a non-positive or non-integer interval, a malformed or out-of-range cron
2371	expression, declaring both an interval and a cron plan, an unknown missed
2372	policy, or an unknown field — is a validation error that rejects the whole
2373	request without partial writes; pausing, resuming, or updating the schedule
2374	of a missing workflow, or pausing and resuming a workflow that has no
2375	schedule, is a missing resource, and a malformed pause or resume body is a
2376	validation error. Querying the schedule change history of a missing or
2377	cross-tenant workflow is a missing resource, and its malformed or missing
2378	`limit`, non-positive `cursor`, unknown or duplicated `action`, malformed
2379	timestamp, repeated or unknown query parameter, and missing or empty tenant
2380	are validation errors, exactly like the price-table change history. Request bodies must not contain
2381	non-finite numbers (`NaN`, `Infinity`, or overflowing values such as `1e400`);
2382	they are rejected with 400. Finite floats keep their full precision, including negative zero
2383	(`-0.0`), and every response body ends with a single newline.
2384	
2385	## Tests
2386	
2387	```bash
2388	PYTHONPATH=src python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
2389	```
2390
